items: Article 19(1)(a) serves as the primary constitutional basis for candidate asset disclosure as established in the landmark ADR (2002) and PUCL (2003) Supreme Court judgments.
Form 26 requires full asset declaration not only for the candidate but also for their spouse and dependents, including liabilities and government dues.
Material non-disclosure of high-value assets can be treated as 'undue influence' on voters, attracting election nullification under Section 123(2) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Candidates contesting elections must mandatorily file an affidavit in Form 26 disclosing movable and immovable assets, liabilities, criminal antecedents, and educational qualifications.
The Supreme Court in Union of India v. Association for Democratic Reforms (2002) established that voter awareness of candidate assets is a fundamental right under Article 19(1)(a).
Section 125A of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 penalizes the submission of false affidavits or non-disclosure of assets with imprisonment up to 6 months, fine, or both.
Civil servants are bound by Rule 18 of the Central Civil Services (Conduct) Rules, 1964 to submit annual declarations of immovable properties.
In Lok Prahari v. Union of India (2018), the Supreme Court held that non-disclosure of asset growth sources amounts to corrupt practice under Section 123(2) of RPA 1951.
